entities.attachmentSummary: Last night, Board of Education President Steven Blair officially welcomed Mark Delaney as the District’s next Superintendent. Delaney, who has served in the interim role since July, will begin his new contract Jan. 1. The agreement runs through June 30, 2028. Blair said the multi-year contract brings stability as the District moves ahead. “With more than two decades of service to Francis Howell, Mr. Delaney is an experienced leader, and one who is respected by parents, community members, and staff throughout the district. He is the right person to lead us into the next chapter and deliver on the goals in our strategic plan.” | DGpQkvwgsvESuV5ZsSdwvyIoQXmJ5oRtgIbJqpY19elZoYqQ4uL5IZ6JFcg4r36ANSJS4qeT6Lx | dtDpAsr.com

Second read and vote will occur at our August 2 9am-1pm Retreat.** Our July Board Meeting is this Thursday. Here’s the agenda. I want to point everyone to Policy 2656. Policy 2656 prevents the use of cell phones and other smart devices during the school day. The Board must pass a policy to align our students’ cell phone use with the new law. entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Hello everyone. Last night’s meeting was shorter than usual. Here are the main updates. 1- Cell phone policy - The governor signed a bill preventing the use of cell phones by students in all schools from bell to bell. Exceptions exist for certain emergencies and if the teachers indicate the phones can be used in their class for educational purposes. We will follow the law and approve a necessary policy at the August 2 Board Retreat Meeting. 2- Francis Howell North Odor - SM Wilson believes they located the source of the odor at FHN. Last school year, a smell would intermittingly show up in certain rooms and hallways. A number of possible causes were explored and addressed, but the smell kept returning. They recently used a pressure measuring device called a manometer. This helped them locate a problem where the building’s pipes connected with the rest of the community. You can hear the longer description by watching the meeting on our YouTube channel. Basically, they are optimistic that they know the cause of the problem and can fix the problem before, or shortly after, the start of school. This sounds like great news which we will all continue to monitor. 3. Dr. Mike Dominguez - I shared last night that the update was that there is no update. We will keep everyone informed as we are able to. We are also thankful for Mark Delaney for stepping in successfully as Interim Superintendent to gey us all ready for the start of school. Thank you everyone for staying involved with our wonderful Francis Howell School District. | l9Nzj1.com

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | From Interim Superintendent Mark Delaney ———— To the Francis Howell Community: Last week, graffiti containing racial slurs and sexual violence was found in restrooms at Francis Howell High School. (See previous communication.) An investigation conducted in partnership with the St. Charles County Police Department found evidence that the graffiti was written by a custodian employed by the District. That individual was immediately placed on leave in accordance with Board of Education policies and regulations, and subsequently arrested by the St. Charles County Police Department and charged with Harrassment Motivated by Discrimination and Property Damage. While the District cannot provide any further details at this time related to confidential personnel matters, I want to take this opportunity to clearly state that racism, hate, and violence have no place in our schools or communities and will not be tolerated. Employees who violate conduct expectations and Board of Education policies face consequences, up to and including termination of employment. I want to express my apologies for this incident and the effect it has had on students, fellow employees at Francis Howell High School, and the broader Francis Howell community. All students and staff deserve to feel safe and welcome at school. You have my commitment that we will continue our efforts to create safe and welcoming learning environments for all students. Mark Delaney Interim Superintendent | zlbRJzl6Ba.com

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Senate Bill 3 is bad for Francis Howell students and staff and bad for our county. It largely freezes property tax revenue by locking in the taxable property value of September 2024. This means that Francis Howell and other school districts, ambulance and fire services, and libraries will have their revenues flatten while all expense continue to inflate. Year one, this would create a $4 million drop in revenue for Francis Howell. By year five, it would create a $20 million drop in revenue. This would decimate Francis Howell and the whole area. Hopefully, the SB3 will be ruled unconstitutional and be removed from the April Ballot. In case it isn’t removed, I will continue to share factual information to make sure it is defeated for the good of every student we are entrusted to educate. This is not a red or blue thing. This is a green thing. Senate Bill 3 takes money away from students and other important services. It is extremely harmful and must be opposed. | ZaRjSR.com

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | From our December Board Meeting 1- We celebrated the State Champion Cheerleading Squad from FHHS. 2- We heard more about our strategic plan and how agenda items are now listed as Pillar 1-4 to help see how we are focusing on our main priorities. 3- We received the report that our annual audit came back ‘clean’ with the highest mark of approval possible. 4- We received our monthly financial report, including information about the negative impact that Senate Bill 3 will cause if approved on April ballot. FHSD will lose $4 million in revenue in the first year and $20 million in year five 5- We unanimously voted to allow the book Viral to remain at the middle school (and high school) level. Viral tells the historical account of the AIDS Virus. 6-We voted on additional language around the school board code of ethics. The new policy 0340 includes progressive steps for a board to vote on largely symbolic responses/consequences 7- We had additional board comments about books and different opinions about what books should be allowed in schools. It was shared that parents already have the right to decide the books their kids read and that a challenge process for books exists, as well. Thank you for reading and staying connected to the great things happening in Francis Howell. | Gi1tv50BpK.com

entities.authorKey: name:steven blair for francis howell school board
entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | The Road Ahead in 2026. In 2026, I will be focused on two priorities as a member of the Francis Howell School Board. First, providing the best education for all students by focusing on our Strategic Plan. Here are the Four Pillars. “Pillar 1- Student Achievement: We will rank among the Top 5% of all K-12 public school districts in the state by 2030.” This includes providing students with the curriculum, technology, teachers, and culture they need to be successful. “Pillar 2 - People and Workforce- We will be a destination district and the employer of choice in the region.” This includes giving teachers and staff what they need to be successful, so that the students will be successful. “Pillar 3 - Finance and Operations - We will be a fiscally sound and efficient organization.” This includes maintaining a balanced budget, diligently valuing every penny, and making financial decisions with the big picture in mind. “Pillar 4 - Safety and Security - All students and staff will be safe and welcome at school and work.” This includes hard work on creating safe buildings and safe environments. My second priority: Defeat Senate Bill 3 on the April Ballot. We will be crossing aisles and joining hands with fire districts, ambulance districts, libraries, Developmental Disabilities Board, and every school district in St. Charles County, all of which lose revenue due to Senate Bill 3. Senate Bill 3 will remove $4 million in funding for Francis Howell in year one. It will remove $20 million of revenue by year five. Senate Bill 3 is a danger to giving students the education and extra curricular experiences they need to succeed. It will pull financial resoirces from our 2000+ employees, impacting salary and benefits and therefore damaging our ability to recruit and retain staff. Senate Bill 3 will also negatively impact building maintenance of our nearly 3 million sq. ft of building space and cause long term capital problems Opposing Senate Bill 3 is not a red thing or blue thing. It is a green thing. SB3 flat lines revenue from property taxes while all other costs experience inflation. Senate Bill 3 damages Francis Howell’s ability to pursue our strategic goals to give the best education to all students. I will keep everyone updated on both the good work happening at Francis Howell and the effort needed to protect Francis Howell students from the damage of Senate Bill 3. entities.authorKey: name:steven blair for francis howell school board
entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | This is a continuation of Update 1 from our May 21 monthly board meeting. 1- We restated our Strategic Plan Goals for 2030. 2- We celebrated the Golden Girls Dance Team from Francis Howell High for winning Nationals in Hip Hop Dance. We also celebrated some ‘High Achievement’ seniors, including Senior Class Presidents. 3-We learned how the therapy dog program at Fairmount Elementary helps students better reset and then re-engage with their lessons. 4- We had zero patron comments. 5- We approved curriculum updates. 6- We approved policy updates. **We discussed two possible ballot initiatives. Because Senate Bill 1002 just passed, St. Charles County School Districts ONLY, are restricted to only being able to place ballot initiatives on even-year November ballots. (SB 1002 also places school board member elections on even-year November ballots and allow candidates to identify their political party). Because of SB 1002, we have to decide how to use the November 2026 Election since our next chance to make changes would be November 2028. Here are two possibilities for November 2026. 1- ‘No-Tax-Increase Debt Service Levy Transfer - This allows us to move funds from one pocket to our Operating Budget pocket to respond to Missouri defunding Francis Howell by $6.1M in 26-27. 2-‘No-Tax-Increase Bond Issue - This allows Francis Howell to pursue needed capital project improvements for our 2.9M sq ft of buildings versus waiting two years and facing inflated costs. I will be sharing more details about both later. For now, I need to acknowledge to the district that we are aware of past problems regarding the funding of FHN and other projects. There has been an audit identifying mistakes and needed improvements. The District has responded swiftly to every directed action. If we choose to go forward with a No-Tax-Increase Bond Issue, we will go forward with the lessons learned from the last one. The public has the right to want improvements made to the process and transparent evidence that the improvements are happening. More on that later, as well, but I wanted to share that we hear you and understand concerns attached to bond issues in Francis Howell. Thank you all for reading and for staying connected to the great things happening in Francis Howell! Happy Summer!! | SP6PY.com

entities.authorDisplayName: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.authorKey: name:steven blair for francis howell school board
entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Meet Wynnie, the first in our new ʜᴜᴍᴀɴꜱ ᴏꜰ ʜᴏᴡᴇʟʟ series. Fourth quarter. 3 minutes, 42 seconds left in the game. Vikings are up. I look to my right and notice a little girl kneeling on the bleachers next to me. She is eye level with the step, clearly searching for something. What did she lose, I wonder? I watch her for a minute, intrigued. She reaches her arm under the bleacher as far as it could stretch, her face smooshed against the metal step. As her arm retracts, I see she’s holding something - a wad of paper. Crumpled up homework, maybe? She marches down the steps and tosses the paper into the trash can. She returns, this time focusing on the student section. Like a human street sweeper, her arms collect empty bottles, paper plates and food wrappers from a sea of teenage feet. Each time, she smiles as she places the trash into the can at the bottom of the steps. She ascends, again. And again. And again, until the game ends. My curiosity finally gets the best of me. As she passes me, I ask why she’s picking up all this trash. She looks at me and says, “Because it needs to be done and I like to help!” I ask if her parents are nearby because I’d love to talk with them. She points to her mom. I learn that the girl’s name is Wynnie, and she’s a first-grader at Daniel Boone. This isn’t the first time she’s picked up trash. Her mom says she attends many of her older siblings’ school events, and she just likes to help out. I tell her what a shining example Wynnie is of the #OneHowell spirit and ask if I can take her picture and share her story to inspire others. With mom’s blessing, I follow Wynnie on her next few trash collection rounds. “Do you think I’ll be on the news?” Wynnie asks. I’m not sure, I say, but the Francis Howell community is going to love you! ʜᴜᴍᴀɴꜱ ᴏꜰ ʜᴏᴡᴇʟʟ is a new series that highlights the remarkable people who make up the Francis Howell community. They live our values and embody the #OneHowell spirit. Know someone who should be featured? Email communications@fhsdschools.org. | NktGjk4I.com

entities.author: Sandy Wilking
entities.text: I was teaching in upstate NY about an hour north of the city… scary times there. We had parents who worked down in the city. I never want to relive those moments again. The fear, the uncertainty, it was unparalleled to anything I had ever experienced. The coming together of America afterwards was a beautiful thing though. Another unforgettable experience.

entities.author: Tori Ross
entities.text: Julie McDonald The cell phone thing is insightful. Smart phones didn't come out until 6 years later. I remember waking up for a late shift at a financial company (don't get me started on moving money out of the stock market for clients that day) and didn't even hear about anything until the towers were already down at around 11 Eastern time. I just didn't turn on the news. If it happened today, I'd open my eyes, check my phone, and probably see 1000 social media posts about it.

entities.author: Julie McDonald
entities.text: Top fanMy first year teaching. I had 3rd grade. I noticed a buzz and parents picking kids up more frequently…but didn’t think much of that because it was an early release day (I think). I guess the principal at the time didn’t want to alarm us, so I didn’t really know until I got home. I turned on the news and saw. I was shocked. Really shows the quickness in speading the word before cell phones. 25 years. Wow.

entities.author: Dena Vitola Dauve
entities.text: I was teaching in Florida at a high school that sits a mile from an Air Force base, that quickly turned into central command. There were huge military planes flying into the base everyday and it was a sight that you could get comfortable with. My kids told me what happened and we just pondered and talk about how it was possible this was happening. A day I will never forget

entities.author: Cristin Spoelstra Ziegler
entities.text: Top fanI was working at Warren and remember kids coming to school saying that a plane hit a building in New York. I wasn’t overly concerned as I thought it was a little plane and though sad, had no idea of the tragedy. Students were getting picked up early, but it wasn’t until we were pulled into the library following a 1/2 day dismissal that I became fully aware of the terrorist attack. We had two teachers on staff whose spouses were pilots. I recall them working frantically to find out where they were and if they were safely grounded.

entities.author: Chad Carron
entities.text: I was teaching at Castlio when I first heard the news from Mr. Votaw. We went to the library and watched the footage online on a computer. We watched the first Tower collapse live. The students were very upset and worried when they got to school and we tried to comfort them and make it like another day at school even though it wasn’t. A few days later, I found out that my high school drivers education teacher from Hazelwood Central , Mr. Salinardi lost his son who was working in one of the Towers when it collapsed. Never Forget!!

entities.author: Renee Rethemeyer Muckerman
entities.text: Top fanI was working at Saeger on that day. It was an early release PD day, so we didn’t really hear all the details because those days were so busy. One of our teachers, whose daughter work in the Federal government, came down our hall hysterical. Her daughter called to let her know she was being moved into the secured bunker in the Rocky Mtns. After we went home it was so bizarre to hear nothing in the air. I live in St Charles and flights take off and land at Lambert in routes over out house.

entities.author: Kelly Heidt
entities.text: I was student teaching a 4/5 grade class in Minnesota. The kids always ate breakfast and watched the news as part of their morning routine.That morning, my supervising teacher stepped out and we watched the second plane hit the towers live. The kids all turned to me for an explanation and I didn’t have one. Just days into my student teaching I realized huge responsibility comes with being a teacher.Within minutes we were told to turn off the TVs and resume our regular schedule.There was only little pieces of new information shared between teachers until the end of the day. That evening I learned a high school classmate was on one of the planes that hit the towers.

entities.author: Becky Hormuth
entities.text: I was an elementary special education teacher in Laurel Maryland which is about 20 miles NE of DC. We were also located 10 miles from Ft. Meade, and 20+ miles from the Pentagon. We had several parents who worked at the Pentagon. I was taking a shortcut to my classroom after a quick RR break through the LC. Our librarian and para were standing under the LC television watching after the first tower was hit. Once the second tower and Pentagon was hit at 9:37 am, shortly after and it was realized that it was a coordinated effort. We went into immediate soft lockdown. Parents in masses arrived to pick up their kids…most all kids were gone by noon. It was such a scary time to be living in that area of the US. #neverforget

entities.author: Traci Bowden Martinez
entities.text: I was at Barnwell. My classroom was a portable behind the school. 8th graders were taking some kind of standardized test, like Explore. My principal walked in and handed me a piece of paper and said don't share this with the kids. I still have that note somewhere. Because no one knew what was going on, I was not allowed to let anyone leave my classroom because they would have been outside. When we were finally allowed to leave our portable, we were ushered in the building by the nearest door very quickly.

entities.author: Jennifer Lynn
entities.text: It was my first year at Howell High. The shock and fear ran through my classroom. We had no computers and no TV in the classroom. One of my colleagues opened my door to tell me. One of my freshman students found out later that her favorite cousin was on Flight 93. She told me her senior year that because I stayed on her case, she stayed in school, and persevered through the trauma.

entities.author: Kelly Iris Turner
entities.text: I was working at Boone Trail Elementary in Wentzville. I had walked into the office, to check my mail before my first class arrived, and something was definetly off. One of the secretaries quickly filled me in. A number of airline employee parents called to reassure their kids that they were okay. Without technology in kids’ hands, however, they had no clue until they got home. The following day the kids were wanting to create art to work through their feelings. A day that will never be forgotten.

entities.author: Raquel Andersen Babb
entities.text: I was working at Crest Ridge just west of Warrensberg, Mo. I was on plan and heard our nurse gasp from her office. When I arrived, the Internet was showing the 2nd plane hit the tower. Then, the Internet froze. Within minutes, we heard a series of sonic booms as the Stealth bombers left Whiteman and went supersonic. Soon after, we heard every plane from that base take to the air. Eventually, a teacher s mom brought us a VHS recording of the Today Show coverage and the principals and office staff took turns covering us so we could see what was happening. My 8 year old was down the road in elementary school, my one year old in daycare in Sedalia where we lived, and my husband was out of town. I thought the world was ending...that a nuke had to be next...and all I wanted was to get my family together in one place.

entities.author: Amalyn Martin
entities.text: I cannot wrap my head around this man simply being out in the community after reading that probable cause statement. According to the filing, he allegedly discussed the bodies of middle school girls, talked about sexual contact with his own daughter, and then characterized these conversations as “fantasy.” What the fuck does that even mean when you are a middle school principal with daily access to children? Even if he is presumed innocent until proven guilty, public safety still matters. When the allegations themselves involve sexual interest in children — especially children the same age as the students entrusted to you — I do not understand why the default is simply “bond out and go home.” If a court has credible evidence that someone may be capable of harming children, that person should not have ordinary access to children while the case is pending. And if they are ultimately convicted, serving a sentence should not automatically mean they are suddenly safe to be around kids again. Treatment, risk assessment, supervision and proof of rehabilitation should matter. And what school district would ever feel comfortable putting someone back around children after even discussing this rancid shit as a “fantasy”? Children should not be the experiment used to determine whether an adult is safe. Protect them first.

entities.author: Emily Johnson van Schenkhof
entities.text: I appreciate you sharing. There is a lot of risk here. To state the obvious, people who view child pornography do so because they have an interest or desire to molest children. The school needs to operate under the assumption that he may have victimized children. The School District has a responsibility to do everything in their power now to make sure their policies/procedures/culture create an environment where child sexual abuse is less likely to occur. My organization, The Missouri's Children's Trust Fund, can help you with this. Please call or email me if you are interested in discussing more. 573-751-9309 or emily.vanschenkhof@oa.mo.gov. It is possible to prevent child sexual abuse but too few agencies/schools take the necessary precautions.

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | You may have heard about an assistant principal being arrested at Hollenbeck Middle School. I am including an email below that Superintendent Mark Delaney sent on Friday so the fuller community can hear. Francis Howell remains fiercely committed to student safety. We will fully cooperate with the investigation and share whatever can be shared so that parents, especially Hollenbeck parents, can feel confident that their students are safe. I am also including a photo of the Post-Dispatch article. ———————————- FHSD Staff, Families and Community: I am writing to let you know that a Hollenbeck Middle School employee was arrested after school yesterday. Law enforcement officers notified the District that Daniel Ott was taken into police custody without incident, and shared their intent to charge Mr. Ott with crimes related to possession of child pornography. Officers confirmed that there is no indication at this time that any Hollenbeck students are involved. Mr. Ott has been employed as an assistant principal at Hollenbeck since 2024. He has been placed on leave pending the outcome of the investigation, and will not be allowed at school or on any District property until the situation is resolved. The safety of our students is our highest priority. This is an extremely serious matter and we understand that the Hollenbeck community has a vested interest in the outcome. Please understand that the District is limited in the information it can share right now due to this being an ongoing investigation. The District will be cooperating with law enforcement to the fullest extent possible to ensure the safety of our students. Thank you, Mark Delaney Superintendent | rlZ1fr.com

entities.author: Stephanie Cooley Rittgers
entities.text: Steve Birk I think there’s two things to keep in mind (probably more as I’m not an expert!). Construction costs have drastically increased since that bond issue passed-which means that the estimated costs that were needed have also probably increased significantly to complete everything on that list. Additionally, we have to remember how many square footage of buildings we have-when we get a new a/c or roof for our hose, the costs are high, but when a school needs those, it’s astounding what the actual cost is. As a parent, I’m really grateful for the updates Prop S allowed the district to do. But our schools still have additional needs. And our kids deserve a place to learn that’s not in disrepair. I look at it as we can get behind the needs of our schools now or we can wait until things are dire-which not only means it will cost more to fix, but also there will be added inflation costs to wait. Neither of these changes the tax rate we are paying-it’s just better use of the resources we have available to us.

entities.text: Of course there are.If you have a 1% tax to cover bonds that expires 10 years from issuance of debt, and the debt is paid off in 6 years then legally the tax remains in place and a fund is supplied with money.One can, instead of simply accruing money in that fund, issue more debt.The tax rate is unchanged, so the bond is a no tax rate bond, rather than flowing into a fund for 4 years that money services debt for use in the now.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Hello Jane. Thanks for the offer. I’d enjoy talking more with you at some point. For this topic, we’ve already had months to discuss any concerns both publicly or privately. I remember another board member sharing a legitimate concern that the change in distribution would not lead to a surge of increased screen time instruction. It was a great question. It was answered that we have a change in distribution and not a change teaching. You helped make this change take place. It improves efficiency for students, saves class time, and saves money for district. I’m glad we were part of the process that made this happen. Good for everyone.

entities.author: Jamie Martin
entities.text: Jane Puszkar Jane, I acknowledge that using computers for every class or even most lessons is not good for learning. Can you acknowledge that computers are needed in the higher grades (not K-5) for students to practice certain tools and tasks?Making sure students have the tool they need for this does not decide the amount of time they are used in instruction. We could even provide guidance that we want that time reduced! But this way, when kids need this tool for a specific task (research, power point, typing an essay), we won’t waste instructional time trying to find a Chromebook for everyone And we can save money by not storing more than we need.

entities.author: Carrie Lea
entities.text: This is great news! I am glad this distribution change was approved. My children graduated last spring, and most of their assignments had some digital component, particularly for homework assignments- creating a presentation, writing a paper or journal response, doing research, or studying using sites like Khan Academy to help understand a math problem more deeply. My kids also frequently collaborated with others on projects for courses or on teamwork in clubs like Speech & Debate and Mock Trial. Having access to programs in the Google suite was extremely valuable for feedback from teachers and collaboration with peers. Without the devices that we purchased ourselves and had at home, my kids would not have had the opportunity to achieve at such high levels, graduating with honors and receiving significant merit awards from their universities. Further, the structure of the courses and resources in Canvas during high school prepared them for how their college coursework is presented and organized at college. They were very prepared and feel confident and read for their semester. Like many of the commenters here, I agree that excess screen time is not good for anyone, adults included. In the past six months, I have started doing more doodling and completing crosswords to keep my screen time down. However, that’s also why assigning the Chromebook to students and allowing them to come home is so important. Class time can be spent with teachers teaching and planning more off screen instruction- like lectures and notes, small group work and collaboration, in depth discussions, hands-on activities, question and answer sessions, and opportunities to use feedback to improve on assignments. Because of this change, the Chromebooks may actually be used less at school and be used more pointedly for homework assignments that give students opportunity to practice what they’ve done in class. ￼The fact that this distribution saves the district money, saves parents hundreds in digital school supplies, and ensures all students have what they need to complete their work seems to be a win-win for everyone. I saw someone comment about computer lab courses with Microsoft programs. FHSD high schools have these courses, and they are awesome. My son took it last year as a senior and learned a lot, preparing him for business school. All work was done on computers in the lab, and I believe you can also earn a certificate for Microsoft programs while in school by taking an exam (he didn’t). It’s so awesome that the high schools have so many awesome opportunities!

It’s always been one of your short falls You still have not addressed the ￼￼research that has been done that confirms that test scores go down, especially when children have a computer screen to stare at all all day. You are going to ruin this district with your lies your half truths and your opinions. Everything you have stated ￼ is an opinion. Provide proof. So far all you’ve done is proved that I was in attendance when the strategic plan was revealed. I’m glad I’m not on the board anymore because I don’t wanna be responsible for the downfall of this district. But you will be. I now have a much better opportunity to reveal your and administrations manipulation of the truth. Stay tuned ￼

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: A change for the 26-27 School Year. We are assigning middle school and high school students their own Chromebooks. This improves efficiency for students and also saves money. Last year, Chromebooks were distributed on a classroom basis. If the maximum amount of students in a classroom was 25, then that classroom needed 25 Chromebooks to be available even if some hours had fewer students. Magnify that situation by the number of all our middle school and high school classrooms and you end up with a lot of extra Chromebooks. Our distribution change improves efficiency so that students don’t have to spend class time obtaining the classroom’s Chromebooks. It also allows the student to more efficiently access their own Chromebook with folders, etc that they know. One student representative at a recent board meeting indicated how much having one designated Chromebook would help students, similar to how much any adult’s job efficiency improves by not borrowing a random laptop every hour during their work day. For added clarity: We are not changing the amount of instructional time students will be on their computer. We are not replacing teachers with computers. Your middle and high school’s access to their own Chromebook is not the result of a spending splurge. We are still managing a $6M loss in state funding compared to what their formula said we were due. We are changing our Chromebook distribution strategy. This results in a better, more efficient experience for student education and reducing cost for the district by reducing the number of Chromebooks that are needed. Thank you to our district IT staff who have worked to recommend and implement this plan. Thank you to building level admin and teachers for their contributions, as well.

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Our August Board Meeting is this Thursday. Here’s a quick preview. 1- We begin with the Pledge of Allegiance led by elementary students. 2- Patron Comments - The Board welcomes hearing directly from the public. 3 - Board votes to approve, or not, a list of items called the ‘Consent Agenda.’ This month, the consent agenda includes the annual adoption of anti-nepotism policies and contracts with different municipalities for our School Resource Officers. 4- The Board will receive its monthly finance report and monthly construction report. These acts are part of the Board’s monthly oversight routine over district finances and capital projects. 5- The Board will vote on the makeup of the 26-27 Policy Committee and Employee Insurance Committee. Members from the public are chosen at random from a list of those who expressed interest. 6- Tennis courts policy - The Board will discuss and vote on a possible change regarding increased community access to tennis courts. 7- Quarterly Updates - The Board will receive a fuller, quarterly update regarding our 2030 Strategic Plan. It includes actions already being made to achieve our goals and an update on next steps. We will also receive the quarterly construction update, another routine providing transparency and an opportunity for Board review. 8- Prop O and Prop H. - The Board and public will receive additional information about these two no-tax-rate increase ballot initiatives that will appear on the November ballot. Thank you for taking an interest in your school district. There are a lot of great things happening in Francis Howell. We would love to have you watch in-person or online. | 94vl8p5CX.com

entities.author: Lauren Nevatt
entities.text: Verna Marie you are right that taxes have gone up, but that isn't from things our district have done. All of those adjustments have been because property values have gone up. In fact, our distict and perhaps others in our county, are capped at what they can receive based on a prior ordinance. In order for the district to receive more money from the tax payers they would need that on the ballot. I would also carefully note that all our our bills are going up as tax payers, so are the bills of the public services (like our schools). They are not exempted from staff wanting more in their salaries, the cost to replace old/broken furniture, purchasing updated curriculum, etc. There is a lot to understand about business of a school district, they have been very open to explaining how they are doing their best to learn from mistakes, adapt new ways of thinking, and doing the best they can with the truly little they receive. But also explaining how the government expects their budgets to operate. I'd suggest when the round table events come out to join some, they have truly been eye opening.

entities.author: Angela Rose
entities.text: Top fanI encourage people of the community to look at what other districts offer and what FHSD has lost over the last 30 years. I started teaching in FHSD in 1996 and saw several rounds of staffing cuts and salary freezes. I moved a year ago 45 minutes away to Illinois and now work in a district where I make $6,000 a year more, 40 fewer students, and double the plan time. I loved FHSD but I couldn’t take the workload, pressure, and apathy from the community anymore. It was so discouraging.

entities.text: Verna Marie the tax RATE legally cannot increase without voter approval. What increases is your Assessed Value, which the School District has zero control over. Further, Francis Howell has one of the lowest rates in St. Charles County. Most other districts are well over 4%.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Steve John Hello Steve. Every, or almost every, school district has bonds. Because we have 23 building and 2.9M sq. ft. of space, bonds will always be needed for upkeep, safety, and efficiency. Looking at the costs shared in an open meeting, passing Prop H in 2026 will save an estimated $20M in expected construction price increases if we tried to approve a bond for the same projects in 2028. I imagine you aren’t suggesting that we stop fixing sidewalks and maintaining HVACS, among other projects. This is the best stewardship of taxpayer money to complete those necessary projects at their lowest costs. We have used past debt service levy monies for debt defeasance in the last 18 months when that action was the best stewardship act as well. Thank you for your questions.

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Update Here are a few items from Thursday Night’s meeting. You can watch the meeting on our YouTube Channel. 1- We approved updated ballot language for Prop H. Prop H is a no tax-rate increase bond issue on the November ballot. The updated language provides clearer information to voters that Prop H will help a variety of capital needs with a clear estimate that it will not raise our tax rate. 2- We discussed tennis courts and how to make them both utilizable for the community while protecting them for their intended student use. Recently, tennis courts have been locked but available for rental. This was in response to a state auditor recommendation about protecting district resources and to align practice with our policy. Administration was following policy by locking the tennis courts. The Board shared a desire for admin to reshape policy to allow for increased access. We will likely discuss and act on options in August. 3- Warren Elementary. The Board had an emergency zoom meeting on Wednesday, July 15th to approve a contract to remove mold at Warren Elementary. The mold was confirmed on July 13 leading to a RFP that presented three options by 5pm on July 14. From there, the Board was asked to meet urgently in order to begin the process of remediation immediately. The Board approved a contract with First Onsite on July 15 allowing the work to begin on Thursday, July 16. The contract could have technically been approved by admin but they rightly decided that this decision would better happen in a publicly available zoom open session, which anyone can also watch on our YouTube channel. The quick actions by admin this week improved our chances to meet that date. 4- There were additional approvals of purchase reports, financial updates, and a first reading for some ELA curriculum. Thank you, everyone. I appreciate you taking the time to stay up to date with the great things happening at Francis Howell. raising their | Oqp0a.com

I appreciate our conversations, both by phone or social media. It’s good hearing from you.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Missouri State Legislators decided not to follow through with their promise to full fund each school according to the funding formula. For Francis Howell, this is a $6M loss of funding in 26-27 (with a $3M loss of funding in 25-26). If Prop O doesn’t pass, it will affect staff pay, staff benefits, and the number of staff positions which impacts class sizes. The last six or more board meetings have pointed this out, which is why the Board decided to put Prop O and Prop H on the November ballot.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Hello Tom. I hope this piece is helpful since there are so many tax conversations and ballot initiatives that they start to blur together. The tax levy for Francis Howell is $3.9769. If Prop O and Prop H pass, the tax levy will be $3.9769.If Prop O doesn’t pass, salaries, class sizes and more will be negatively effected. If Prop H doesn’t pass, our next chance to get bonds approved will be November 2028. The identified needed projects will cost an estimated $20M more at that time. Passing Prop O and Prop H allows for wise stewardship of taxpayer funds to provide a great education for students WITHOUT raising the tax rate.

entities.text: If there is truly no additional cost to the community in voting yes on both measures, then a “no” vote would be difficult to justify as anything other than a lack of support for the community’s needs and future success.What is most concerning is that staff compensation cannot simply be adjusted through state funding alone. Schools continue to face challenges from state promises that go unfunded, reductions in available revenue sources, and ongoing changes to the tax system that limit local funding options. At the same time, this community consistently expresses a desire for strong schools and quality programs, yet has historically been reluctant to approve tax increases that would provide meaningful financial support. If these measures fail, the district may not have another opportunity to seek assistance from the community for up to two more years, making this decision especially important for the future of our students, staff, and schools.

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | We have a BIG Update. Last night, the Board voted unanimously to add Prop O and Prop H on the November 3rd Ballot. You will be receiving ongoing updates explaining the details of each over the next few months. Here is an important, brief overview. Points #1-5 - No Tax Rate Increase! - Our tax levy is $3.9769. If either, both, or neither Props pass, our tax levy will be $3.9769, the lowest in St. Charles County. Point #6 - Prop O is a "No Tax Rate Increase Debt Service Levy Transfer." Tax Revenue either enters a school district's pocket (fund) that pays operating expenses or one pays down debt. Due to Missouri legislators' recent decision, Francis Howell will receive $6M less in funding than their funding formula instructed them to give. Passing Prop O allows us to to maintain class sizes, extracurricular activities, and staffing in the wake of this defunding. Point #7 - Prop H is a "No Tax Rate Increase Bond Issue" A Facility Master Plan was approved as a road map in early 2026. We have 2.9M sq. ft or buildings that need to be maintained and updated. The planned projects would cost an estimated $24M of taxpayers dollars MORE if we wait another two years to start these projects. Note: The Board is aware of concerns and mistakes associated with the previous bond for Francis Howell North. At last night's board meeting, we shared lessons that were learned from earlier mistakes as well as the steps we have been taking ever since to prevent similar problems. This includes policies requiring regular updates to the public and Board at Board meetings about construction projects and controls around greatest maximum price. Passing Prop H secures the necessary funding to pursue this plan. Each project still needs to be bid out for competitive bids and be approved by the Board in public session. We will continue to share the improvements that we have been implementing over the last few years. Point #8 - Why November 3rd? Missouri legislators recently passed SB1002 that applies ONLY to St. Charles County school districts. It limits SCC school districts to place ballot measures only on even-year November ballots. We have been sharing information about Prop O and Prop H (without the titles) for over a year with April 2027 in mind. Due to SB 1002, we are placing Prop O and Prop H on the November 2026 Ballot. Passing Prop O and Prop H does not cost the public any additional money. Rejecting Prop O and Prop H will damage Francis Howell's ability to provide adequate classroom sizes, salaries, extracurriculars as well as efficient, safe, and well-maintained buildings. Please ask any questions and I will do my best to answer them. The voters will get a chance to decide what type of education they want for kids. With No-Tax-Rate Increases: On November 3rd, Vote YES on Prop O. Vote YES on Prop H. ONE HOWELL!!! Watch here https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=kEK40mn8s1A&pp=ygUsZnJhbmNpcyBob3dlbGwgc2Nob29sIGRpc3RyaWN0IGJvYXJkIG1lZXRpbmc%3D&ra=m | 8RF3eHXs.com

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Preview At our June 18th Board Meeting, we will continue with many of the basic actions of the Board. This includes reviewing, questioning, and then voting on a personnel report, travel requests, agreement with two municipalities regarding School Resource Offers, food service contract, and renewal of our fuel agreement for our buses. Discussing and approving a budget in June is one of those regular acts. Major sections of the budget has been presented to the Board over the last few months, including the full presentation at our June 4th special session. This June 18th meeting will have two significant new agenda items. 1- Debt Service Levy Transfer - Prop O This is a No Tax Increase Tax Levy Transfer ballot initiative. It shifts money from our debt service pocket to our operating expense pocket. This will allow us to use funds on pressing operating expense needs following the Missouri Legislator providing $6M less funds than the state funding formula promised. 2 - No Tax Increase Bond Issue. - Prop H Again, no taxes are being increased. Prop H will allow us to fund capital projects and pursue them before construction costs increase any further. Due to Senate Bill 1002. St. Charles County school districts, and ONLY SCC school districts, can only place levy and bond issues on even year November ballot. There are significant problems with SB 1002, but we are making good financial choices even with its unique restrictions. A Prop H bond issue would cost significantly more if we pursued it during 2028. These two ballot initiatives will shape Francis Howell for the better. Vote for One Howell Yes on Prop O and Prop H in November.

entities.author: Michele Dunaway
entities.text: Your retirees are another concern. We pay 100 percent of the costs to stay on the plan until eligible for medicare, and while that's fair, it's also become problematic as this year a retiree pays $1121 per month ($821 and then $300 per month for deductible average). You cannot retain quality teachers when they know that their PSRS benefits will be reduced by a cost of $13,452 a year for health insurance. From 24/25 to 25/26 the cost went up for retirees by around 2400. PSRS pension went up $100 a month, or $1200. Can't wait to see how much it goes up next year. This means that retiring costs a teacher real money. To meet this cost, the district does offer retired teachers the option to sub, but retired teachers must spend approximately 61 days subbing in the district to meet the cost of their healthcare. You cannot keep and retain good teachers if the end goal is not sustainable for them--not just as salaried employees, but retired employees, and without good retiree benefits, many teachers will stay in the district much longer, at higher salaries, as they cannot afford to leave. And that's its own set of problems.

entities.text: Stephanie Drilling board members have stated openly that all is not well financially.For the past 2 (3?) years we’ve been burning through a reserve and these recent cuts have exacerbated that (on top of rising healthcare costs)Over 80% of the operating budget is salary and benefits because we are, in fact, ridiculously cut to the bone on spend.IMO we should cut some of the other 20% and just take those hits. Make it clear that no, there isn’t waste. Any cut impacts the district negatively.Stop transfers to capital and allow facilities to fall apart.Cut the SROs, $1M+ in security theater pays a lot of benefits.But instead the staff will be asked to sacrifice and he long term hurt for the district will be worse. It just won’t be obvious that it’s because we, as a district (voters) are too cheap to pay teachers and uphold a reasonable level of benefits.

entities.author: Stephanie Drilling
entities.text: Thank you for the explanation. However, I remain skeptical about the proposed “No Tax Increase Debt Service Levy Transfer” and “No Tax Increase Bond Issue” for November. Francis Howell already has very healthy reserves — over $172 million in total governmental fund balances as of June 30, 2025, with operating funds still well above your own minimum policy targets. The district also benefits from one of the stronger local property tax bases in the region. Past “no tax increase” bonds, especially Proposition S ($244 million in 2020), promised major projects at certain costs but delivered significant overruns. The new Francis Howell North High School, for example, went from an advertised ~$86 million to over $164 million — nearly double — according to the State Auditor’s report. That led to dozens of other promised projects being cut or delayed, and the district received a “poor” rating on transparency. Before asking voters for more borrowing capacity or shifting levy dollars from debt service to operations, I’d like to see: A detailed, independent accounting of current outstanding debt and exact remaining Prop S funds. Concrete evidence of cost controls and better project management going forward. Clear prioritization: Why can’t the district live within its substantial existing revenue and reserves before shifting more money around or issuing new bonds? Full disclosure on how much this would extend debt payments and what the long-term impact on the tax rate could be (even if called “no increase” now). “No tax increase” language often masks shifting burdens or extending repayment periods. With healthcare costs and state funding issues being real challenges, the focus should first be on efficiency, transparency, and living within our means — not floating new ballot measures so soon after the last expensive round. I appreciate you communicating, but taxpayers deserve full candor on these financial maneuvers.

That led to dozens of other promised projects being cut or delayed, and the district received a “poor” rating on transparency.Before asking voters for more borrowing capacity or shifting levy dollars from debt service to operations, I’d like to see:A detailed, independent accounting of current outstanding debt and exact remaining Prop S funds.Concrete evidence of cost controls and better project management going forward.Clear prioritization: Why can’t the district live within its substantial existing revenue and reserves before shifting more money around or issuing new bonds?Full disclosure on how much this would extend debt payments and what the long-term impact on the tax rate could be (even if called “no increase” now).“No tax increase” language often masks shifting burdens or extending repayment periods. With healthcare costs and state funding issues being real challenges, the focus should first be on efficiency, transparency, and living within our means — not floating new ballot measures so soon after the last expensive round.I appreciate you communicating, but taxpayers deserve full candor on these financial maneuvers.

entities.author: Ewan Ross
entities.text: I'll go ahead and reiterate that I get this is hard. I also want to reiterate that the public at large isn't going to feel the pain (or acknowledge it as the source at least) of this. Choices that actually impact the public are unfortunately the only ones that are going to drive change. Get rid of SROs (what's that, like $1M). Don't provide any service that isn't education adjacent and costs even a penny. Or at least make it clear that if we can't get staff onto a path where their benefits aren't getting wrecked every year then this is what will happen next. Nobody cares about being competitive with adjacent districts. It doesn't matter. Every school district in the nation needs good teachers. All our teachers could just go work in the private sector. Cuts to benefits that exist are a pay cut. Simple as that. Employees honestly give zero hoots about the hidden cost to the district - you take $100 out of their paycheck every month, that's what any employee in any industry sees. And that harms the relationship between employer and employee. Irreparably. Bus routes can be reverted to normal. Services can be restored. SROs can be brought back as easily as they are got rid of. Staff morale isn't going to spring back, even if you get the resources in 1-5 years to return benefits to where they were. We ask teachers and staff to sacrifice every damn time. It's past time that we, the voting public, sacrifice if we aren't collectively willing to step up.

entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Update 1 from the May Board Meeting Last night, the Board approved the district’s employee insurance plan. Here are some important details. 1- FHSD has a ‘Self-insurance Plan’. This allows us more autonomy to edit plans but also means the district is on the hook if the cost of benefits exceeds the income from premiums. Last year, the benefit costs exceeded premium income by $11 million, removing a cushion for this year. 2- Health insurance costs continue to skyrocket nationwide. 3- Missouri State legislators chose to not fully fund the formula by an amount of $3.2M for 25-26. They are reducing further this year (26-27) by an additional $6.1M. That leads to $9.3M in lost revenue over two year. We know our District cares about Staff and Teachers. To address rising insurance costs, over the last few years employees have increased their contribution by 2.9%. The district has increased its contributions by 67%. I voted to approve the district’s recommendation of Option 2.5. Here’s why: 1- Years ago, FHSD froze salary increases and paused giving teachers their ‘Steps.’ BECAUSE OF THE STATE’s DEGREE of DEFUNDING, we are too close to the fund balance amount that preceded those drastic budget measures to continue with our current plan. 2- The approved Option 2.5 Plan still exceeds the plans in our neighboring St. Charles County School Districts. This gives us a competitive advantage in recruiting and retaining teachers and staff, a priority shared by our unions. For the ‘Base Plan’ Employee Only Plan - District still pays 100% of your premiums Employee + Kid(s) - District pays 63% of premiums Employee + Spouse - District pays 47.8% of premiums Employee + Family - District pays 44% of premiums. (Wentzville and Ft. Zumwalt pay 0% of premiums for kid, spouse, and family) We are thankful to the public for defeating Prop RT 59% to 41% in April, otherwise we would have $4M less this year. The Board is also considering a No Tax Increase Debt Service Levy Transfer and a No Tax Increase Bond Issue for November. These actions would allow us to address the severe drop of State funding and pursue the needs listed in our Facility Master Plan before construction costs inflate further. I wish the numbers were different. I, and other board members, wrestled with this decision. We especially considered its impact on employees with lower salaries/wages. We unfortunately had to make this change. The reserves to cushion rising costs were already spent last year ($11M). The revenue from the State has already been decreased by a total $9.1M for 25/26 and 26/27. We have to make decisions based on the money we have and not the money that was promised. I wanted to explain the context behind the change and will be glad to answer other questions. Like you have hopefully seen in previous months, I will continue to work for the funding our students, staff, and schools need. | c1VZe.com

entities.authorKey: name:steven blair for francis howell school board
entities.attachmentSummary: ShowMe | Preview for the May 21st monthly Board of Education Meeting. 1- We will receive an update on district work related to Pillar 2 of our Strategic Plan which focuses on Teachers and Staff. 2- We will celebrate the Golden Girls Dance Team, a section of High Performing Students, and the Fairmount Elementary Therapy Dog Program. 3- Employee Insurance Plan Approval - The Board will discuss plans presented by the Employee Insurance Committee. We will hear the thorough process the committee engaged in for six months. This will be a difficult conversation due to rising health care costs and reduced state funding. Speaking personally, I am valuing a plan that both allows us a competitive advantage in recruiting and retaining employees in St. Charles County and valuing a plan that does not risk future budget measures of freezing raises or delaying ‘steps.’ 4- No-Tax-Increase Debt Service Levy Transfer. School districts have the ability to redirect tax revenue from going into the pocket reserved for debt service into the pocket used for its operating budget. This would have to be approved by the public at the ballot. We will discuss the timing of the possible ballot measure due to the passing of SB 1002 which limits school-related ballot measures to even-year Novembers. 5- No-Tax-Increase Bond Issue. The Board will discuss the timing of a no-tax-increase bond issue to help us pursue our Facility Master Plan. The impact of SB 1002 will inform this conversation, as well. Item 4 and 5 are Information items and will not be voted on at the May 21 Meeting. 6- Report of State Funding Change - With the state legislature session ending, we will receive a report on the amount of decreased state funding we should expect. Thank you everyone for reading. We would love to have you join us in person or watch online at 6:30pm this Thursday. | A0DDNp.com

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: I believe we need less Washington DC political partisanship in school districts. Some people thought we needed more. SB 1002 was just passed in Jefferson City against bipartisan opposition. St. Charles will stand alone in Missouri as the one county where school districts could be known for the political party of its board members instead of the accomplishments of its students. That is not good. If the purpose of SB 1002 was only increasing voter turnout, they would not have included a provision allowing board candidates to identify their political party on the ballot. SB 1002 is blatantly partisan and also impractical. It confines all school-related tax and bond issues to even year November elections even though state legislators can decrease funding to schools at anytime. Some people want more Washington DC political games in school districts. This will only hurt students and the quality of their education. I will continue to advocate for a nonpartisan approach to create the best public education for all students in Francis Howell.

entities.author: Matthew Paul
entities.text: Kristin Clemons Your response to the school board is a perfect example of right wing identity politics operating under the guise of simple common sense. While you and others on the political right frequently complain about identity politics on the left you are playing the exact same game here by defining your own specific cultural group as the default baseline for what is natural and correct. By framing your demands around valuing families you are not actually talking about all families in the district but are instead using that phrase as a protective shield to signal to a specific conservative voting base. You position your own deeply ideological viewpoint as the standard of human life while labeling anyone who disagrees with you as an outside threat pushing an artificial and damaging progressive agenda.Your post relies heavily on a strategic trap known as belief bundling where you wrap up completely reasonable educational concerns in the exact same package as aggressive cultural warfare. You try to hook the school board by leading with valid points that almost any parent or taxpayer in this county would agree with such as focusing district funds on classroom teachers instead of sports stadiums and supporting staff with student behavior. However you intentionally package these practical goals alongside highly volatile attacks regarding sexual agendas. This is a deliberate attempt to force the school board into a corner where addressing basic school operations is treated as inseparable from endorsing your specific right wing cultural crusade.The most manipulative part of your message is your deliberate effort to trigger a high arousal state of fear regarding the safety of children. When you demand an end to what you call the insanity of putting mentally struggling individuals into supervisory roles you are using dehumanizing language to target a specific group of people such as trans staff or school counselors. By presenting this to a school board member you are trying to create an artificial emergency where the safety of local children is framed as being at immediate risk. Once you introduce this level of fear into a public discussion it shuts down rational debate and forces people to retreat behind defensive walls which is exactly how your brand of identity politics operates to divide our community.This interaction shows exactly why the school board should refuse to take your bait and enter into a cultural boxing match with you. If the board responds by launching an equally intense identity defense they validate your narrative that the school system is just a battleground for competing lifestyles. A universal strategy wins by completely unbundling your argument and agreeing wholeheartedly with your sensible points about teacher support and financial transparency while entirely ignoring your inflammatory cultural traps. When the board consistently demonstrates that it respects all families and focuses on practical education your entire right wing identity firewall collapses because the fear you are trying to feed has nothing left to rely on.

entities.author: Ted Macinski
entities.text: I’ve lived here my entire life… caring is not in the vocabulary here. Friendship is always transactional here, kindness is something I’ve rarely witnessed. People hated me in school, they hate me in the community, they hate everything about me. Yet they know nothing. They look at me and see something that weighed doesn’t exist or is so distasteful that they would regularly wish me dead through school. Do you really want me, who is not a traditional Christian, who believes in the teachers to do the right thing, who believes librarians can figure out what’s appropriate, who was kicked out of high school, who despite that was accepted to major universities, who became an alcoholic due to loneliness and dis acceptance from this awful community, voting fora board member? I would love to see the kind of money wasted by Francis Howell spent on the schools damaged by the tornado downtown. I would love to see actual community outreach. If it wasn’t for a few very lucky factors in my life I would be homeless here. You don’t want my vote. I have time to read. I have time to reach out and talk to representatives. I have time to search their social media history. I have time and I see it as a tool to cause disturbance where freedom to understand the self at any age is disrupted by those wishing to impose their will on others.

entities.text: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board I think school boards would be better if they valued families, took the concerns with sexual agendas seriously, made learning about learning academic content, supported teachers so they didn’t have to spend so much time and energy on behaviors and worrying about whether they will be supported, focused finances on their teachers versus stadiums and facilities and stopped the insanity of putting mentally struggling individuals into supervisory roles with children. I wish it weren’t so, but sadly political ideology has deeply infused public education.

entities.author: Heather Fleming
entities.text: Haley Geno, people serving on school boards do not need to be nonpartisan in their personal or professional lives. The election process should be nonpartisan and their school board work should be based upon what is best for the district, not what aligns with their party view. For instance, I'm progressive. However, as an educator, if a student wrote an essay about being conservative, I didn't grade it based upon whether I agreed with them. I used the same rubric for all students and scored it for structure, peer-reviewed sources, grammar, syntax, etc. Everyone has viewpoints; nonpartisanship is about your reasoning and actions.

However, as an educator, if a student wrote an essay about being conservative, I didn't grade it based upon whether I agreed with them. I used the same rubric for all students and scored it for structure, peer-reviewed sources, grammar, syntax, etc. Everyone has viewpoints; nonpartisanship is about your reasoning and actions.

entities.text: JJ Suftko, from their personal page, they can advocate for whatever they feel aligns with their values. That is their First Amendment right as American citizens. Voters can decide if their values align with their candidates. From their official board pages, I expect to only see what directly impacts the students, faculty staff, and families of the district, as Steven is doing here. That can sometimes mean asking people to withdraw support if that business isdoingso.ething detrimental to the district. I answered your question in good faith, although it does not appear to have been asked in the same spirit. Who is employed at the business was irrelevant to the issue at hand. Board members can support students without spending money at businesses that support Trump. In fact, that person's performance as a board member is what's most relevant in this situation. In his/her official duties, are they making decisions that benefit all students? Are they supporting faculty and staff? Are they showing up? Are they nonpartisan in those instances? That's what matters.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Grant Kilen If you want more information in the voters hands, you would want the elections in April. Millions by state and national partisan politics will flood mailboxes and inboxes. The vast majority of November voters will not see the information being put out by school board candidates and school district ballot initiatives. Giving board candidates the chance to identify their political party means people will vote for or against someone just because of the R or D by their name. You would be a good school board member. Imagine thousands of people judging your ability because of your party affiliation. It didn’t matter how often you showed up to support the schools of how willing to work with others who might disagree. It didn’t matter what you did with the little money to raised because all your messaging was lost in the millions of dollars of noise. The only information that thousands of people would use to vote is a candidate’s political party. We need less Washington DC partisan politics in schools, not more.

entities.text: Sherry McNail Hello Sherry. I appreciate the conversation. In April 2023, candidates from FH Families won a decisive victory with 9000+ votes for candidates. In 2026, FH Families candidates had a similar number of votes but lost handedly to those who had 12000+ votes. Increase turnout happened in April. It just wasn’t the voters that some Missouri Legislators wanted so some want to change the rules. Also, if the main purpose was to move to November to increase voter turnout, why the effort to allow board candidates to identify their political party? It’s clear there is a partisan reason behind SB 1002.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: SB 1002 would make St. Charles County the only county in Missouri that allows school board candidates to identify their political party ballots, move school board candidate elections to even year Novembers, and confine school-related bond issues to even year Novembers. Its advocates say the change is about voter turnout. 1- Allowing candidates to identify their political party on the ballot is not connected to voter turnout. 2 - The reasons candidates lost in April 2026 who won in April 2023 is because of increased voter turnout. The turnout in April 2023 was large enough that it was called a ‘mandate.’ The problem is that the wrong voter turnout increased. Rather than changing messaging or recruiting more volunteers, supporters of the recent candidates that lost created SB 1002. If you can’t beat them, change the rules. 3- Yes, more people vote in November because people are compelled by state and national elections and issues. School board issues are at the bottom of the ballot. School board members will do what they can to push through the millions in advertising hitting our mailboxes and inboxes but pragmatically, information about school and school board candidates will be hard to push through the noise. 4- SB 1002 confines all school-related tax levies and bond issues to even year Novembers. No company would restrict their ability to respond to emerging needs in this way. This piece of SB 1002 is incredibly impractical and doesn’t reflect knowing about school district administration. Again, SB 1002 only impacts SCC. We will be known as having the most partisan school districts in the state. Districts in SCC will be known by whether they are ran by donkeys or elephants. We need less partisan politics in school districts and not more. Call your representative today. Or, call someone else’s representative who is wise enough to not add their county onto this bill.

I'm pointing out that some board members do that and some don't and it's great that we now have 7 who don't, allowing this discussion to occur here. entities.text: Sherry McNail I didn't say all show up informed, but your implying that none do is just not a valid argument. I would also say that there is the distinct possibility that we're trading who you say are uninformed voters with their "union cards" (which happened to benefit one of the FHFam candidates, as memory serves) for uninformed voters showing up and making decisions based on a letter after a candidate's name in November. I prefer a candidate discuss their policies, not their party. April elections force them to do that.Further, there are very good reasons having to do with the budget, the fiscal year, and when the school year starts that support April elections for school board.If this were the smart move the legislators claim it is, they wouldn't be isolating it to school board but would be expansing it to other municipal elections. The fact that they are limiting this to schools, and that no other county thinks this is a good idea, says something.BTW, isn't it cool that you can come on this page and disagree with Mr. Blair and not get blocked? I personally like public servants who allow everyone's comments, even those who disagree, and who can speak respectfully to everyone they're working for.

entities.author: Steven Blair For Francis Howell School Board
entities.text: Grant Kilen Hello Grant. I appreciate your feedback. In April, Missouri Legislators placed SB 3 (Prop RT) on our ballot. It would have led to a $4M defunding of revenue in year 1, $7M defunding in year 2, and will grow to a $20M funding in year 5. Imagine losing that funding in an odd year and having to wait 18 months to an even year November for even the chance to replace lost revenue. There are multiple bills being discussed this week that can defund Francis Howell by an estimated $5.5M. Unless Missouri Legislators will decide to only vote on measures to defund public schools in even year Aprils, St. Charles School Districts need to have the flexibility to respond to Jefferson City whenever a bad bill that hurts St. Charles schools is passed.

entities.author: Matthew Paul
entities.text: Pushing for local issues to remain on a local stage is not about being partisan. Instead, it is about acknowledging that school board elections deserve their own dedicated stage. This keeps them free from the overwhelming noise of national politics. When we move these races to a November general election, we risk turning complex district issues into afterthoughts at the bottom of the ballot. In that environment, choices are often made based on broad political labels or simple name recognition rather than a deep understanding of the specific needs of our schools.The reality is that voters who show up for an April election demonstrate a higher level of intentionality and engagement. These are the community members who have done the work to research the candidates, understand the budget, and follow the challenges unique to our district. They are not at the polls because a presidential ad told them to be. Rather, they are there because they have a demonstrated interest in the direction of our local education system.Ultimately, keeping school board elections in April is not about excluding anyone. It is about ensuring that the people steering our schools are the ones most invested in the nuances of local governance. Our children’s education and our community’s future are far too important to be treated as a secondary thought in a massive and intensely polarized general election cycle.

When we move these races to a November general election, we risk turning complex district issues into afterthoughts at the bottom of the ballot. In that environment, choices are often made based on broad political labels or simple name recognition rather than a deep understanding of the specific needs of our schools.The reality is that voters who show up for an April election demonstrate a higher level of intentionality and engagement. These are the community members who have done the work to research the candidates, understand the budget, and follow the challenges unique to our district. They are not at the polls because a presidential ad told them to be. Rather, they are there because they have a demonstrated interest in the direction of our local education system.Ultimately, keeping school board elections in April is not about excluding anyone. It is about ensuring that the people steering our schools are the ones most invested in the nuances of local governance. Our children’s education and our community’s future are far too important to be treated as a secondary thought in a massive and intensely polarized general election cycle.

You don’t think November voters can decide who gets their vote for president and BOE at the same time? That’s too much to expect of someone? Wild. I didn’t know the Fort Zumwalt gal spelled her name with a K. I see it spelled Erica everywhere else. Odd.

entities.text: GO bonds are meant to be for long-term financing. Urgent needs can be financed with TANs by a simple majority vote of the board at any time. Tax increases are meant to be permanent measures for future needs not temporary solutions for an urgent problem. Actually that’s the whole point of TANs. The legislature has constructed a scheme wherein the board acting alone can address urgent, temporary needs, but the consent of the voters is required for decisions of long-term fiscal policy.

entities.author: Matt Stolle
entities.text: Amy Fonte That’s a good question.Yes, many cities will still hold their own April elections for mayor/council.But moving school board races to November still saves the district and taxpayers real money. Right now, April is often a low-turnout, school-heavy election that the district largely pays for (polling sites, judges, ballots, staffing).In November, those costs are shared across a huge ballot with many more races and voters — the district only pays a fraction. Fewer separate ballots, fewer extra workers, lower per-voter cost.That’s the direct savings. Plus, higher turnout means less control by small organized groups.

entities.author: Henry Kriss
entities.text: The receipts are in. If you are a teacher who has ever written a dues check and assumed it was going toward better pay, stronger benefits, or a decent contract, read carefully. A new report from Defending Education has blown the lid off one of the most brazen political money machines in American history, and your money is in it.Since August 2015, the National Education Association (NEA) and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) have funneled a combined $669,324,912.33 in member dues and PAC funds into left-wing political entities, far-left nonprofits, and Democratic campaigns. Fold in state and local affiliates, and the total surpasses $1 billion.The big money tells the story. The State Engagement Fund, a Democratic Party infrastructure vehicle, received $60,525,000. The For Our Future Action Fund took $44,732,078. The Senate Majority PAC received $32,655,000. The House Majority PAC got $25,842,790. The Strategic Victory Fund, created in 2020 explicitly to defeat Donald Trump, received $19,300,000.On top of all that, the unions pumped over $85 million directly into Democrat Party entities at every level of government, not counting a single dollar in individual candidate contributions. The Biden Victory Fund received $923,500. The Hillary Victory Fund got $444,250. The Bill, Hillary, and Chelsea Clinton Foundation collected $725,000, with another $400,000 to the Clinton Global Initiative.https://redstate.com/ben-smith/2026/04/29/teachers-dues-became-a-1b-democrat-slush-fundnot-classroom-funding-n2201843

entities.text: Julia Bietsch In fact, we spent several years canvassing in March/April and also volunteering outside the polls. I also served as Mark Ponder’s campaign treasurer. entities.author: Randy Cook Jr.
entities.text: The desire to move school board elections to November is much older than Francis Howell’s recent Progressive candidate wins on the school board. Steven Blair is simply wrong and misleading his constituents. I went back 5 years to look for all of the bills that would have moved school board elections to November. There have been several bills. This isn’t a new thing.In 2021, see SB 150 (Onder), HB 920 (Baker), and SB 414 (Brattin).In 2022, see SB 740 (Eigel), HB 2306 (Christofanelli).In 2023, see SB 234 (Brown)In 2024: see HB 2536 (West)In 2025, see SB 485 (Schroer), HB 539 (West)It took me 15 minutes to prove he was wrong on this. If only he would do his own research before spouting lies to the community.

entities.author: Mindy Darrow
entities.text: My biggest concern with changing to November - besides the face this billl ONLY APPLIES TO ST CHARLES COUNTY which is ludicrous…is that it will financially tie the hands of every area public school district. We will be limited to asking for tax initiatives in Nov every 2 years vs every April where it stands now. In addition, school budgets are set in June. So this means a board that votes on the budget won’t be the same board that manages the budget for the full year.
